                               RESPONSIVE BRIEF OF
                 INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMER ORGANIZATIONS AND AMTRAK

           Pursuant to the Order on Show Cause Proceeding, Directing Compliance Filings,

Establishing Paper Hearing, and Granting In Part and Denying In Part Complaint (“Order”) in the

above-captioned dockets,1 and the January 23, 2026, Notice of Extension of Time,2 the PJM

Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJMICC”), the Industrial Energy Consumers of America

(“IECA”), the American Forest and Paper Association (“AF&PA”) (collectively, “Industrials”),

and the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (“Amtrak”) hereby file this Responsive Brief in

response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’

(“PJM Transmission Owners”) Initial Briefs in Docket No. EL25-49, et al. (“Initial Briefs”)3,

which were filed at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) on

February 23, 2026, in the above-captioned dockets.

                                   I.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

           As retail customers with high energy consumption needs, the Industrials/Amtrak have long

endorsed customer choice as a foundational principle for electric service. As such, the

Industrials/Amtrak appreciate the promise of new transmission services designed to support the

type and amount of service required by customers. Lessons can be learned from the optionality in

the natural gas industry, while also recognizing the utility’s obligation to serve and the right of

industrial, institutional, and transportation customers to receive reliable electric service under

various federal and state laws. The proposed implementation of PJM’s three new transmission

services (“New Services”) may yield benefits and optionality, but the New Services must be just,

reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential under Section 206 of the Federal Power

Act.4 Consequently, implementation of the New Services requires careful consideration of

regulatory and jurisdictional issues and adherence to cost-causation principles. As the Commission

develops the details for the New Services, the Industrials/Amtrak emphasize the following:

           1) A just and reasonable back-up service is missing from the new transmission services
           structure. Back-up service provided without a default assumption that it will be used during
           system peaks is guaranteed to Qualifying Facilities (“QF”) under the Public Utility
           Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (“PURPA”) and should be extended to other retail
           customers with on-site generation on a cost-causation basis, either through retail netting or
           through a firm, back-up service charged on a cost-causation basis (“cost-based”).

           2) The outcome of PJM’s pending compliance proposal in FERC Docket No. ER26-1479
           (“BTMG Compliance Docket”) regarding PJM’s retail Behind-the-Meter Generation
           (“BTMG”) applicability rules, including a yet-to-be-determined materiality threshold
           (“Retail Threshold”), directly impacts and relates to the New Services and whether the
           terms and conditions of the New Services are just and reasonable. While specific eligibility
           for retail netting is under consideration in the BTMG Compliance Docket, no firm cost-
           based back-up service has been proposed in the instant proceeding.

           3) The Commission should incorporate incentives for Co-Located Load to bring new
           generation, with appropriate inducements for such generation’s reliable operation.

          4) The terms for New Services must respect state/federal jurisdictional boundaries and
         clearly translate into transparent retail rates.

         Industrial retail configurations are varied, complex, and unique. Generally, in contrast to

typical computational loads, industrial customers produce a physical product on-site; cannot shift

load to other facilities; often must continue to operate for safety and environmental compliance

reasons; and frequently have generation and load deeply integrated via cogeneration, a process that

generates both electric power and useful thermal energy.5 Traditional industrial load

configurations with BTMG also provide substantial benefits to the grid—this traditional, existing

customer load did not trigger the current resource adequacy challenges on the grid, nor does it

present the reliability risks posed by super-sized loads rapidly seeking to come online today. In the

BTMG Compliance Docket, the Industrials/Amtrak submitted the Affidavit of James R.

Dauphinais (“Dauphinais Affidavit”), in which Mr. Dauphinais provided testimony concerning the

configurations of industrial, institutional, and transportation retail customers, particularly QFs, and

the technical and regulatory basis for ensuring such customers have access to back-up power at

just and reasonable rates.6

         In contrast to the “traditional” load described above, computational loads (including data

centers) do not generally have substantial cogeneration, typically do not operate large motors

(which can help with grid stability), can turn on and off nearly instantaneously, and can reach

extremely large sizes, well beyond most traditional industrial and institutional retail customers.

The size and scale of the computational load currently in the planning process across PJM is

            As most planned load growth is driven by load additions greater than 300 MW, the

Industrials/Amtrak proposed in the BTMG Compliance Docket a Retail Threshold of at least 200

MW, under which BTMG netting should continue.7 The Industrials/Amtrak also proposed that

QFs maintain their continued eligibility for BTMG netting, in accordance with PURPA

in the design of the New Services becomes a heightened concern.

            Retail customers represented by the Industrials/Amtrak in this docket seldom grab

headlines and are often not at the center of large-load and transmission planning discussions

grown up around such traditional loads, worked in concert with them, and benefited from their

presence, operations, and long-term planning. As explained further in Section III, infra, these retail

and must be understood to ensure just and reasonable determinations in this proceeding.

            Examples are plentiful. For some retail customers, industrial processes with cogeneration

and combined heat and power (“CHP”) assets may require steam heat produced from the

generation, meaning if the generation goes down, the load follows. In that case, it would defy cost-

causation principles to require such a facility to pay for transmission services it cannot physically

           Other industrial customers currently qualify, or could qualify, as QFs under PURPA,

granting them the right to back-up and maintenance power at rates/terms that do not assume that

units will be down during system peaks and do not assume that units will be down at the same time

as the other QFs (unless there is data backing that assumption). Yet, as will be explained further

herein, the current proposed design of the New Services in the Initial Briefs makes no allowance

for back-up power at cost-based rates.

           A third example is that, as a legacy of the buildout of the Northeast Corridor (NEC),

Amtrak requires service at 25 Hz, which it receives, at least for some of its requirements, through

a contractual arrangement with a third-party generator that is neither a small power production QF

nor a cogeneration QF. This arrangement provides the only black-start capability for Amtrak’s

south end of its Northeast Corridor traction power system if the 60 Hz power grid goes out of

service.

           Each of these configurations, plus others, is described in greater detail in Section III, infra.

These configurations underscore the critical need for the FERC to consider the impact on

traditional large-load configurations to ensure a just and reasonable replacement rate when

authorizing a final design for the New Services. Absent a just and reasonable method of obtaining

back-up power, many retail customers will face devastating economic consequences. For some, as

further explained below and in the Dauphinais Affidavit, it will mean closure of generating units,

exacerbating the current resource adequacy concerns in the region.

this result is avoidable. The Commission can authorize the New Services while also ensuring a

just and reasonable back-up service is in place for QFs and other similarly situated retail customers.

Accordingly, the Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request that the Commission develop the New

Services, consistent with the comments and changes recommended herein, to ensure the avoidance

of unintended and irreparable damage to America’s essential manufacturing sector and

institutional and transportation service providers.

                                       II.     BACKGROUND

           On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued the Order, finding that the PJM Tariff is

unjust and unreasonable due to the lack of specificity for the rates, terms, and conditions that apply

to Co-Located Load and directing PJM to make several compliance and informational filings. The

Order directed PJM to create three New Services, including an interim, non-firm Network

Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”), a Firm Contract Demand Service (“Firm

CDS”), and a Non-Firm Contract Demand Service (“Non-Firm CDS”).10 Paper hearing procedures

were established to evaluate the rates, terms, and conditions of the New Services.

           The Order also addressed PJM’s retail BTMG rules, which have long allowed for

measurement of a retail customer’s transmission (as well as capacity, energy and ancillary

services) cost responsibility by actual use of the system as measured at the meter. In light of its

finding that “circumstances have changed since the Commission approved PJM’s retail BTMG

rules,” the Commission directed PJM to implement changes to BTMG rules above a yet-to-be-

determined materiality threshold (“Retail Threshold”).11 PJM, the Industrials/Amtrak, and others

                                III.     THE INDUSTRIALS/AMTRAK

that offer essential medical and educational services. In many cases, these traditional institutional,

industrial, and transportation customers own or operate their own generation—not because energy

is their primary industry, but because their core work is energy-intensive. These customers have

elected to construct or contract for retail BTMG in order to control their own energy costs, create

efficiencies, and/or address reliability needs. Even though the Order was issued largely in response

to the impacts of “super-sized” loads such as data centers on the grid, the resulting changes (as

currently proposed in the Initial Briefs) will directly and deeply impact these traditional retail

            To that end, the Industrials/Amtrak respectfully request that the Commission consider the

following arguments in determining rates, terms, and conditions of the New Services. With the

changes recommended herein, the Commission can approve rules that effectuate the goals of the

Order while avoiding unintended damage to America’s essential manufacturing sector and

institutional and transportation service providers.

                                        IV.    ARGUMENTS

           A.       A just and reasonable back-up service is missing from the new transmission
                    services structure. A cost-based back-up service is guaranteed to Qualifying
                    Facilities under PURPA and should be extended to other retail customers with
                    on-site generation on a cost-causation basis.

           The New Services represent a significant change to how transmission services are

designed, bundled, and paid in the PJM region. However, as currently proposed, the New Services

are missing a critical component. The current design lacks a back-up service that is based on cost-

causation and that meets the legal requirements of PURPA. Back-up service is an essential

component of energy management for many industrials and other retail customers with on-site

generation, including QFs, which are guaranteed access to back-up service with specific cost-based

assumptions.24

           Because neither the New Services nor NITS calculated on a gross basis meet these

requirements, as explained below, at a bare minimum, QFs should retain access to longstanding

retail BTMG netting rules. If the FERC determines otherwise, however, the FERC should ensure

QFs have access to a cost-based back-up service. Retail customers with BTMG that is not a QF

should also, based on principles of cost causation, be provided with access to cost-based back-up

services, either through NITS with netting or through a cost-based back-up service. Access to

 back-up services is a critical component to allowing industrial, institutional, and transportation

retail customers to continue to operate without significant economic damage, including likely

closures of some BTMG generating units.

                    1.       PURPA ensures that QFs have access to back-up and maintenance
                             service that meets assumptions about generator uptime, and the NITS
                             netting construct meets this requirement.

           Congress passed PURPA in 1978 to encourage cogeneration, small power production, and

geothermal energy production.25 PURPA has played an important role for manufacturers and the

electric grid for nearly five decades, providing market access where none previously existed,

taking strain off the grid, and supporting American industry by enabling economic means to reduce

energy costs. Under PURPA, QFs fall into two broad categories: “qualifying small power

production facilities,” which can be sized up to 80 MW, and “qualifying cogeneration facilities,”

which have no size limit.26 Cogeneration QFs must achieve certain efficiency standards and are

highly efficient in their use of input fuels. Cogeneration QFs, which produce both electricity and

heat from the same fuel source, make use of the “waste heat” in their manufacturing, heating, or

cooling process. As explained by Mr. Dauphinais in the attached Affidavit (which was filed in the

BTMG Compliance Docket), “Cogeneration Facilities can achieve efficiencies in excess of 80%,

by using waste heat and avoiding electrical losses, compared to the efficiency of approximately

50% for conventional electricity generation with a steam boiler.”27

           Under FERC regulations (enacted at Congress’ direction), QFs are entitled to access to

supplementary power, back-up power, maintenance power, and interruptible power, pursuant to

            Critically, rates for back-up or maintenance power “[s]hall not be based upon an

What are Cogeneration Facilities?

       5.        FERC defines a Cogeneration Facility to be “equipment used to produce electric

energy and forms of useful thermal energy (such as heat or steam), used for industrial,

commercial, heating, or cooling purposes, through the sequential use of energy”.3 Given that on

a combined basis these facilities provide both thermal and electric energy, cogeneration facilities

are also commonly referred to as Combined Heat and Power (“CHP”) facilities.

       6.        There are two types of Cogeneration Facilities – Topping-Cycle Cogeneration

Facilities and Bottoming-Cycle Cogeneration Facilities.

       7.        FERC defines a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility as “a cogeneration facility

in which the energy input to the facility is first used to produce useful power output, and at least

some of the reject heat from the power production process is then used to provide useful thermal

energy”.4 A common example of a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility would be a facility

with combustion turbine generation fired by natural gas, combustible waste gases, or some

combination of the two, that produces electricity and provides steam for heating, cooling, and/or

industrial processes via heat recovery steam generators that collect waste heat from the

combustion turbine generator. Another example would be a facility with boilers fired by fossil

Cogeneration Efficiency

       10.     As I have noted, FERC’s definition of Cogeneration Facility requires the

“sequential use of energy”.8 Specifically, for a Topping-Cycle Cogeneration Facility, FERC

requires “the use of reject heat from a power production process in sufficient amounts in a

thermal application or process to conform to the requirements of the operating standard”,9 where

the “operating standard” is “the useful thermal energy output of the facility must be no less than

5 percent of the total energy output during the 12-month period beginning with the date the

facility first produces electric energy, and any calendar year subsequent to the year in which the

facility first produces electric energy.”10 For a Bottoming-Cycle Cogeneration Facility, FERC

requires “the use of reject heat from a thermal application or process, at least some of which is

then used for power production”.

       11.     Cogeneration Facilities, which, as I have noted, are also commonly referred to as

CHP systems, are typically highly efficient because they capture heat that would otherwise be

wasted and avoid electrical losses by generating electricity at the location where it will largely, if

not entirely, be consumed. Specifically, Cogeneration Facilities can achieve efficiencies in

excess of 80%, by using waste heat and avoiding electrical losses, compared to the efficiency of

approximately 50% for conventional electricity generation with a steam boiler.11

and the Critical Need for Reliable Backup and Maintenance Power at Just and Reasonable

that I have discussed, Cogeneration Facilities are typically highly integrated with the industrial

processes, commercial processes, heating processes and/or cooling processes of their host retail

customer. This has four major implications.

       14.     First, there is a need for very high availability from the Cogeneration Facility to

meet the host retail customer’s thermal energy needs in order to assure the retail customer can

operate its commercial or industrial processes that require thermal energy or to assure the retail

       15.     Second, the electrical output of the Cogeneration Facility can be much less than or

much greater than the electrical load of the host retail customer. This is because the thermal

energy needs of the retail customer typically dictate how much electric power must be produced

by the Cogeneration Facility. For example, if an industrial retail customer has a very high steam

need for its processes relative to its electrical needs, the Cogeneration Facility serving that

contrast, if an industrial retail customer has a very limited steam need for its processes relative to

its electrical needs, the Cogeneration Facility serving that customer will likely produce electric

power well below the level that the retail customer needs for its electrical load. This requires

that the retail customer be able to purchase supplementary (or supplemental) electric power to

cover the deficit from either a utility under a regulated retail electric service rate or from the

wholesale power market through a retail supplier at just and reasonable rates where retail

customer choice is available.

       16.     Third, when an outage of Cogeneration Facility occurs, significant electric load of

the host retail customer can be lost immediately following, or very shortly following, the outage

either due to certain retail customer industrial or commercial processes not being able to operate

       17.     Finally, most relevant to this current proceeding, there is a very high need for the

Cogeneration Facility to be able to purchase reliable backup and maintenance electrical power

economically meet the needs of its own customers and clients. If that ability cannot be assured,

cogeneration may fail to be a practical and/or economic solution to the retail customer’s needs,

causing the efficiency benefits of cogeneration to be forgone and/or the retail customer to

become economically unviable.

III.    COMMERCIAL, INDUSTRIAL AND INSTITUTIONAL CUSTOMERS USING
        COGENERATION ARE NOT THE SAME AS VERY LARGE
        COMPUTATIONAL LOADS CO-LOCATED BEHIND THE METER OF
        GENERATION FACILITIES

        22.     Very large computational loads co-located behind the meter of generation

facilities are not similarly situated to traditional large commercial, industrial and institutional

loads using Cogeneration Facilities located behind their meter.

        23.     In particular, very large computational loads by their very nature generally do not

have a high thermal energy need relative to the magnitude of their total electric load and do not

produce large amounts of waste heat relative to the magnitude of their total electrical load. As

such, they are not candidates for Cogeneration Facilities beyond potentially addressing their

cooling and heating needs.

        24.     Thus, very large computational load processes are generally not highly thermally

integrated, if integrated at all, with the co-located generation facilities whose meter they may be

located behind. This is because those generation facilities will either not be Cogeneration

Facilities or be Cogeneration Facilities of greatly limited electrical capability relative to the total

magnitude of the electrical load of their host retail customer.

        25.     Without such integration, the co-located generation facilities will not provide the

efficiency benefits that are provided by Cogeneration Facilities in serving commercial, industrial,

and institutional customers. In addition, depending on the specific nature of the co-located

generation facilities, the generation may be operated only intermittently rather than at the high

capacity factor typically required of Cogeneration Facilities to ensure their host retail customer

thermal process needs are being reliably fully met.
